title: Coffee and a pastel de nata in Lisbon
setting: It's mid-morning in Lisbon's Alfama district. You step into a small pastelaria (pastry shop). Locals stand at the counter with a quick coffee, and trays of golden pastéis de nata sit behind the glass.
objectives: Get a pastel de nata just how you like it
Say thank you correctly in Portuguese
varietyNote: This is European Portuguese as heard in Lisbon. It sounds quite different from Brazilian Portuguese and uses different everyday words — an espresso is a "bica" in Lisbon, but just "um café" in much of Portugal and a "cafezinho" in Brazil (see the Rio adventure).

phrases.translation: Go ahead! / What can I get you? (literally "say")
phrases.example: —Bom dia, diga! —Bom dia, uma bica, por favor.
phrases.exampleTranslation: "Morning, what can I get you?" "Morning, an espresso, please."

phrases.example: Uma bica e um copo de água, por favor.
phrases.exampleTranslation: An espresso and a glass of water, please.

phrases.translation: a milky coffee served in a tall glass
phrases.example: Um galão e uma torrada, por favor.
phrases.exampleTranslation: A milky coffee and a slice of toast, please.

phrases.example: —Mais alguma coisa? —Um pastel de nata, por favor.
Um pastel de nata com canela e açúcar em pó.
phrases.exampleTranslation: A custard tart with cinnamon and icing sugar.
phrases.note: Pastéis de nata are often sprinkled with cinnamon and/or icing sugar — you can add your own.

phrases.exampleTranslation: Thank you, have a good day!
phrases.note: The ending agrees with the person speaking: men usually say "obrigado", women "obrigada" — whoever they're thanking.

cultureNotes: Having a quick coffee standing at the counter ("ao balcão") is very common, and often cheaper than sitting at a table or on the terrace.
An espresso is the default coffee. If you want a large milky coffee, ask for a "galão".
Portuguese people appreciate any effort in Portuguese. Speaking Spanish and assuming it's "close enough" can come across badly — English is a better fallback.
"Obrigado" or "obrigada" depends on the speaker, not on who you're thanking.

steps.text: You squeeze in at the counter. The man behind it nods at you.

steps.speaker: Server
steps.translation: Good morning! What can I get you?

options.text: Go ahead — what would you like?
options.why: Literally "say", it's the everyday counter invitation to order.
He's not asking for your name — he's inviting you to order.
"Wait a moment" would be "um momento". "Diga" means go ahead.

steps.prompt: You'd like an espresso, Lisbon-style. What do you ask for?

options.why: "Bica" is what Lisboetas call an espresso. "Um café" works anywhere in Portugal too.
"Cafezinho" is Brazilian. You'll be understood, but it marks you as having learned Brazilian Portuguese.
A galão is a large milky coffee in a tall glass — not an espresso.

steps.prompt: You can't resist the custard tarts. What do you say?

options.text: Sim, um pastel de nata também, por favor.
options.why: "Yes, a custard tart as well, please." Perfect.

options.text: Sim, um pastel de nata. Rápido!

options.why: That means "nothing else, thanks" — you'd miss out on the pastel de nata!

options.text: Cinnamon to sprinkle on your pastel de nata
options.why: Right — cinnamon (and icing sugar) are the classic toppings.
A napkin is "um guardanapo". "Canela" is cinnamon.
He's offering cinnamon, not more coffee.

steps.text: You want to ask how much it is, but you can't remember the Portuguese words.

steps.prompt: What's the best thing to do?

options.text: Try simple Portuguese ("Quanto é?") or switch to English — not Spanish.
options.why: Right. Any effort in Portuguese is appreciated, and English is the better fallback.

options.text: Switch to Spanish — it's basically the same language.
options.why: Portuguese and Spanish are different languages, and assuming they're the same can come across badly.

options.text: Leave money on the counter and walk out.
options.why: No need — just ask "Quanto é?" (How much is it?).

steps.prompt: You pay and want to say thank you. Which word do you use?

options.text: It depends on you: men usually say "obrigado", women "obrigada".
options.why: Right — the ending agrees with the person speaking, not the person being thanked.
"Obrigado" is what men usually say; women usually say "obrigada".
A common mistake! It depends on who's speaking, not who you're thanking.

steps.speaker: Server
steps.translation: Thank you! Have a good day!
